name: Spanish Plateresque

revival_periods.note: Spanish neo-Plateresque, used for university and civic buildings at home and for Spanish pavilions abroad.

Arrives in California and Florida as the 'Churrigueresque' portada — the ornamental-panel-against-plain-wall device, which is Plateresque in origin, generally misattributed. Goodhue's California Building at San Diego, 1915, is the hinge.

lineage.note: The ornamental vocabulary — grotesques, candelieri, medallions, balusters, putti, shell niches — arrives with Italian craftsmen working in Spain from the 1490s and with engraved sheets, and is handled with real technical understanding. What does not arrive is the Italian sense that ornament should be regulated by an order.

Underneath a Plateresque facade the building is very often Mudejar: brick construction, a par y nudillo or artesonado timber ceiling, tile paving and dado, and a carpentry trade unchanged since the 14th century. The two coexist in the same buildings continuously and the kit genuinely blends.

Columns, pilasters, entablatures and arches appear as a quoted surface repertoire framing the registers of a retablo facade. They are never used structurally and never regulate the building; this is quotation, not descent.

description.short: A Spanish ornamental system in which Italian Renaissance detail is compressed into a bounded, altarpiece-like panel of extraordinary density set against an otherwise blank ashlar wall.
description.long:
Plateresque is usually explained by its name — from platero, silversmith, so 'in the manner of a silversmith' — and the name is misleading. The style is not fine or small-scale in the way metalwork is; it is the exact opposite of small-scale, because its whole effect depends on a very large area of absolutely plain golden ashlar against which a very small area of hallucinatory carving detonates. The right analogy is not the silversmith's bench. It is the retablo, the carved and gilded altarpiece that stands behind a Spanish altar: a bounded rectangular field, divided into horizontal registers by cornices and vertically by columns or balusters, filled edge to edge with figures, medallions, heraldry and grotesque, and framed by a hard moulding that stops the whole thing dead. Plateresque takes that object off the sanctuary wall and puts it on the outside of the building, and the proportional system of the facade is retablo proportion, not classical proportion.

This is why Plateresque behaves so strangely by Italian standards. A Florentine palazzo facade is regulated throughout: string courses, window rhythm, cornice, and quoins are all part of one system, and ornament is distributed. A Salamanca facade has a plain wall with three or four small windows placed where the rooms need them, and then a single vertical explosion three or four registers tall around the door, which has almost no relationship to the fenestration behind it. Spain had received the Italian repertoire as a set of motifs rather than as a discipline, and — more importantly — Spain already had a late-Gothic Isabelline habit of doing exactly this, concentrating carving on a portada and leaving the wall alone. The Italian motifs simply replaced the Gothic ones inside a Spanish compositional habit that did not change.

The moment is short and the reasons for its end are documented. Plateresque belongs to the first half of the sixteenth century, the boom decades of Castilian confidence, university foundation and American silver, and it is essentially over by 1560. What kills it is the arrival of a genuinely disciplined classicism under Philip II — Juan Bautista de Toledo and Juan de Herrera at the Escorial from 1563 — which brings the Vitruvian regulation Spain had previously declined, and which produces a reaction so severe that estilo desornamentado, the 'unornamented style', becomes the court manner within a decade. Spanish architecture swings from the most decorated surface in Europe to the barest, in one generation, on the same peninsula.

Standing in front of a Plateresque facade in low sun is an experience of pure relief-depth. The Salamanca stone is a soft golden sandstone that carves like cheese and hardens on exposure, so the undercutting is extreme — five and six centimetres deep in places — and the shadow does the work. From across the plaza the portada reads as a dark textured rectangle. From ten metres you begin to resolve the registers. From two metres it dissolves into a legible programme of heraldry, portrait medallions, saints and inscriptions that a literate sixteenth-century Spaniard was expected to read like a page. And two metres to the left of it, the wall is empty.

defining_characteristics: Ornament confined to a bounded field — portada, window surround, patio arcade, cresting — with the great majority of the wall left plain ashlar
Retablo composition: the ornamental panel divided into two to five stacked horizontal registers by cornices and framed by a hard vertical border
Italian Renaissance motif vocabulary — grotesques, candelieri, medallions, putti, shell niches, balusters — executed in deeply undercut relief
Heraldry as a compositionally load-bearing element, usually anchoring the upper register
Classical columns and pilasters used as framing devices only; they never carry a real entablature across the whole facade
Arcaded patio on slender columns with basket or Corinthianising capitals, and a carved or wrought balustrade above
Mudejar construction and carpentry behind the classicising skin — brick walls, artesonado ceilings, tile floors
diagnostic_tells: A wall that is more than half empty, with all the carving in one vertical strip around the door
Relief so deeply undercut that at midday the portada reads black
Coats of arms of a size that makes no compositional sense unless you understand they are the point
Scallop-shell niches and roundel portrait medallions used as repeating units within a register
A cresting (cresteria) of pierced stonework or pinnacles running along the parapet, unrelated to any roof behind it

distinguished_from.difference: A century and a half later, and further gone. Churrigueresque uses the estipite — an inverted-obelisk pilaster — as its module, breaks and doubles every cornice, and dissolves the framing members into the ornament. Plateresque keeps its frames crisp and its registers legible.

Italian work regulates the whole facade by an order and distributes ornament across it. Plateresque leaves the facade unregulated and concentrates ornament in one panel. The motifs are shared; the compositional method is opposite.

Mudejar is brick, geometric, non-figural and produced by a continuous Islamic craft. Plateresque is stone, figural, humanist and quoted from Italy. They occupy the same buildings routinely, which is why they need distinguishing rather than merging.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Retablo, not order. The module is the ornamental panel and its frame: total portada width sets the register heights, and the columns or balusters within it are dimensioned to fill their register rather than to any canonical ratio of diameter to height. The plain wall around it has no proportional system at all — its openings are placed by the rooms behind them.
typical_ratios: Portada width to height roughly 1:2 to 1:3, in two to five registers
Ornamented area 15-40 percent of the principal elevation; plain ashlar the remainder
Relief depth 40-80 mm on the principal field, undercut
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: A single dominant vertical portada, symmetrical about its own axis, flanked by blank wall. The window rhythm of the building is independent of it and frequently in conflict with it, and the conflict is not resolved.

massing_affinities.note: The colegio, convento and palace are all fully enclosed arcaded patios; the portada is the one point where the block addresses the street.
Three-sided courts in smaller palaces and hospitals.
The cross-plan hospitals of Enrique Egas (Santa Cruz, Toledo; Santiago) are effectively an H or a Greek cross with courts in the angles.
Urban palaces sit in continuous blocks, but the style is almost never applied at row-house scale.

constraints.statement: Ornament must be confined to a bounded field with a hard frame. At least 60 percent of any principal elevation must remain plain ashlar. Distributing the ornament destroys the style outright.

Columns and pilasters frame registers; they must not carry a continuous entablature across the facade. If a real order regulates the whole wall, the building has become Italian Renaissance or Herreran, not Plateresque.
The portada is applied dressed stone carried on the wall behind, typically 300-600 mm deep. It is not a structural frontispiece and must not be modelled as one.

test.note: Tests the applied-portada-depth range, the same reading as churrigueresque.c04. 'Not a structural frontispiece and must not be modelled as one' stays prose.

constraints.statement: Heraldry is required and must anchor the composition, normally in the upper register. A Plateresque portada with no arms is missing the reason it was paid for.

Where the interior carpentry is Mudejar — artesonado, par y nudillo, tile dado — it must be allowed to remain so. Coffering a Plateresque building in the Italian manner is a common revival error and a historical falsification.

exemplars.name: Hospital de Santa Cruz
exemplars.note: 1504-1515, Enrique Egas; the transitional building, with a Gothic cross plan, a Plateresque portada and a Renaissance patio.
exemplars.why: The Spanish article's own periodisation separates the vaulting from the front -- the facade, main patio and zaguan doors built 1515-1535 on a building begun before 1514 -- which is the transitional case the node's exemplar note claims, stated by a source rather than asserted.

exemplars.name: Universidad de Salamanca, principal facade
exemplars.note: c. 1512-1529; the canonical retablo facade, three registers of villamayor sandstone against a plain wall, with the medallion of the Catholic Monarchs at its centre.
exemplars.why: 'Para muchos, esta fachada es la obra maestra del plateresco español' -- an attribution the article makes to many readers rather than to itself, and the same article states the three cuerpos this node's own description depends on.

exemplars.name: Convento de San Esteban
exemplars.note: Facade begun 1524 by Juan de Alava, completed 1610; a Plateresque portada at cathedral scale under a Gothic-vaulted church.
exemplars.why: Its own source says the front 'se concibió como un gigantesco retablo', which is this node's central thesis -- that a plateresque facade is altarpiece proportion and not classical proportion -- stated of a real building by somebody else.

exemplars.name: Ayuntamiento de Sevilla
exemplars.note: 1527-1564, Diego de Riano; the fullest civic application, with grotesque pilasters and medallion friezes over the Plaza de San Francisco front.
exemplars.why: The fullest civic application, and the one exemplar whose source describes plateresque relief covering two whole storeys rather than a bounded portada; that is the node's own claim running the other way, and the record says so.

exemplars.name: Palacio de Monterrey
exemplars.note: Begun 18 January 1539 to plans by Rodrigo Gil de Hontanon and fray Martin de Santiago, executed by Pedro de Ibarra and Pedro de Miguel y Aguirre; never finished, the standing building being a fragment of a much larger project. BIC RI-51-0000332, 6 May 1929.
exemplars.why: Added by Tranche 3 as the plateresque PALACE beside three institutional fronts, and because its register reference is the firmest in this cluster -- a code and a declaration date printed twice on one page.

exemplars.name: Casa de las Conchas
exemplars.note: 1493-1517; a late-gothic urban palace with plateresque elements, its street wall studded with carved shells and its courtyard of about 18.8 by 16.8 m carrying mixtilinear arches on Carrara marble columns.
exemplars.why: Added by Tranche 3 because it is the only building in this node whose source states a LINEAR dimension -- the other five records in this node carry counts or nothing -- and the dimension is of the courtyard rather than of the portada -- which is the evidence gap this cluster kept meeting, and is better recorded than left implicit.

sources: Kubler & Soria, Art and Architecture in Spain and Portugal and their American Dominions 1500-1800
Marias, El largo siglo XVI: los usos artisticos del renacimiento espanol
Chueca Goitia, Historia de la arquitectura espanola: Edad Moderna

proportion_packs.note: Secondary. The arcade here is a patio arcade on slender columns -- 'column slenderness 7-9 diameters' with 'basket or Corinthianising capitals, and a carved or wrought balustrade above' -- so the pack's column rules govern rather than its pier rules. What this pack does NOT carry is what this record is actually about: 'ornament confined to a bounded field -- portada, window surround, patio arcade, cresting -- with the great majority of the wall left plain ashlar'. That bounded-panel ornament logic is its own item on WP-4.1's candidate list and is untouched here.

THE NODE THAT NAMED THIS PACK BY NAME. Its `moorish-arch` binding note ends: 'WP-4.1's own portada/retablo gap is the pack Plateresque actually needs and it is still missing.' Its `vignola-tuscan` note declines the same work -- bound 'NOT for the ornamental panel, which no order pack in the library should be forced onto' -- and its `facade-arcade` note says what that pack does not carry is 'what this record is actually about'. Three notes, one gap. This node supplies the module itself ('the module is the ornamental panel and its frame'), the 1:2 to 1:3 aspect, the two-to-five registers, the applied depth, the heraldry requirement and the independence rule. The estipite rules do NOT apply here and the record says so: Plateresque never uses the member.

Judgment binding, bound narrowly. spanish-plateresque is not in vignola-tuscan's own applies_to, and this style's own proportional_system is explicit that the portada is retablo, 'not order' -- so this is NOT bound for the ornamental panel, which no order pack in the library should be forced onto. It covers only the patio arcade's column shafts: this style's own typical_ratios give 'patio arcade column slenderness 7-9 diameters,' which brackets Vignola's Tuscan column at 7 diameters closely. It does not cover the capitals, which this style's own text calls 'basket or Corinthianising' inventions rather than correct Tuscan capitals -- shaft proportion only.

Judgment binding, same reasoning and same doubt as the equivalent binding on churrigueresque. Not in room-harmonic's own applies_to, but its parent family 'spanish-classical' is. This style's own text gives slightly more support than churrigueresque's does: the proportional_system states outright that the plain wall's 'openings are placed by the rooms behind them,' i.e. the building genuinely has ordinary rooms following an ordinary logic independent of the portada -- this pack is offered as the best available (not a good) account of what that ordinary logic might be, for a style contemporary with the early Italian Renaissance whose vocabulary it explicitly imports (lineage edge to italian-renaissance, weight 0.4).

Judgment binding, and a narrow one. Plateresque is a classical-order style with Mudejar survivals in it; the order packs already bound govern its apparatus. This pack is bound secondary for the alfiz and the polylobed arch where they appear, and for nothing else. WP-4.1's own portada/retablo gap is the pack Plateresque actually needs and it is still missing.
